title: Wrath and patience
hookLine: anger isn't wrong in itself; rage that wants harm is

lines: DOEST THOU WELL TO BE ANGRY?
cards: A prophet is furious with God. Jonah was sent to warn the great city of Nineveh, he finally went, and it worked. The people turned around, and God spared them.
And Jonah is livid. Listen to why. He prays: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger, and of great kindness."
That's his complaint. He's angry that God isn't angry. And God answers with one short question: "Doest thou well to be angry?"

teach.h: BE YE ANGRY, AND SIN NOT.
teach.b: He doesn't say, never be angry. He asks whether this anger is doing well. That's the line Christian teaching draws: anger itself is not the sin.
Mark's Gospel says Jesus once looked round on a room "with anger," and in the same verse, that he was grieved.
Paul writes something close to permission: "Be ye angry, and sin not: let not the sun go down upon your wrath." So where's the line? The old teachers put it here.
Anger rises at something wrong, an injustice, a cruelty, a lie, and that can be clean: the energy that makes a person stand up for someone.

teach.h: WHEN IT WANTS HARM, IT'S WRATH.
teach.b: It turns into wrath when it stops wanting the wrong fixed and starts wanting someone hurt. When it rehearses the argument at two in the morning. When it keeps score.
Paul's sunset is a deadline: don't carry it to bed. The answer the tradition gives is patience, and the Bible's phrase for it is the one Jonah threw back at God: slow to anger.
A psalm says it of God: "The LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy."
Proverbs makes it a kind of strength: "He that is slow to anger is better than the mighty; and he that ruleth his spirit than he that taketh a city." Slow, not never.
The anger can still come; it just doesn't get to drive.

teach.h: SWIFT TO HEAR, SLOW TO WRATH.
teach.b: James puts it in a sequence anyone can try: "swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to wrath." Hear first. Speak later.
Get angry last, if at all.

how: Christian teaching on the deadly sins names wrath, anger that seeks harm, and pairs it with patience; some Christians bring a grudge to confession or prayer, and some make a habit of settling a quarrel before the day ends, after Ephesians 4:26.

o: a loud voice, and waiting quietly in long lines
any angry feeling, and never getting upset
anger that wants harm, and being slow to anger

games.q: slow, not never — tap the pairs.
p: angry that God spared the city
let not the sun go down upon your wrath
swift to hear, slow to speak
better than he that taketh a city

s: the Bible treats every kind of anger as a sin
Paul writes "be ye angry, and sin not." anger turns to wrath when it wants harm.
Jonah was angry because God was merciful
he says it himself: "I knew that thou art a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger."
"slow to anger" is said about God in the Psalms
"the LORD is merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and plenteous in mercy."

games.q: you're Jonah. the city you warned has been spared, and you're furious about it. God asks, "doest thou well to be angry?" what do you do?
o: go out of the city and sit down to see what will happen to it.
go back in and warn them again.
games.why: Jonah doesn't answer. he walks out, builds a little shelter east of the city, and sits to see what will become of it. the book ends with God still asking him questions.

practice: Bring back one small thing that made you angry this week, a driver, a reply, a tone of voice, and before doing anything with it, count ten slow breaths. Somewhere around six or seven, ask Jonah's question: is this anger doing well?
If you pray, you can hold the psalm's words: slow to anger, plenteous in mercy.

wordCard.voice: Wrath and patience. Anger that wants harm, and the strength to be slow to anger, the way the psalm says God is.

orig.note: Hebrew: slow to anger, the phrase in Jonah 4:2 and Psalm 103:8.

carryVoice: Your line: slow to anger. Not never angry; just slow. Until tomorrow.
